explanations.explanation: This feature is a detector for the “�” replacement character (U+FFFD) – essentially the model’s signal for an invalid or unknown‐byte/​unrecognized glyph in any script. It fires whenever the tokenizer has to insert that placeholder for a malformed or out-of-vocabulary character.

This feature fires on the final “.” when it ends a short, standalone fragment used as a title/heading or list label—e.g. bulletin-style headings, section titles, numbered captions, forum‐subject lines—rather than inside a running sentence.

The feature fires on the literal “.” when it’s used as an internal punctuation mark rather than as a sentence-ender—e.g. the dot after a single-letter initial (M. D., J. Lee), state or month abbreviations (N.Y., Nov.), directional/place codes (N. Monroe), domain or module names (Node.js), copyright notices, multiplication dots in math, etc.

This neuron fires on the “head” content‐word of a sentence or phrase—i.e. the main noun in titles and definitions (program, mask, Regiment, components, rate, etc.) or the principal verb in headlines (slows, stick, produced)—highlighting the single term that carries the core concept or action across diverse technical and formal contexts.

explanations.explanation: This feature lights up on capitalized name-fragments across both prose and code—things like month abbreviations (Oct), personal or brand names (Steve, Dre, JetBra​ins, CafeMom), special identifiers (__future__), class/library names, browser names (Explorer), court-document terms (Pleas), etc.—in short, it marks tokens that serve as proper nouns or titled identifiers.

Here’s a one‐line abstract for each feature (highlighted token) grounded in its contexts:

• work – the notion of “work” as a topic or activity, whether scientific labor in study titles or praise/feedback in code‐review threads  
• living – a lifestyle or way‐of‐life heading, often eco‐ or well‐being–oriented (“Green living,” health/personal growth lists)  
• thought – marking personal reflection or mental content (e.g. “thoughts I do not want to keep in my head,” site navigation/reviews)  
• leads – a causal‐link signal in news headlines (“X leads to Y”), framing events → consequences  
• Everyone – a universal quantifier pronoun introducing broad claims or generalizations in both news and informal posts  
• molasses – a culinary ingredient label (e.g. “molasses thickener”) in food‐and‐drink write-ups  
• air (airs) fares – travel‐booking jargon around low‐cost flight searches and pricing deals  
• series – product‐line descriptor in fashion copy (“series blazer,” matching suit separates)  
• expert – professional‐status tag in news award headlines (“Genetics expert Francis Collins…”)  
• story – the label of a feature article or cover piece in magazine/journalism contexts  
• environment – the deployment or testing setting (industrial, software, lab) in technical/industrial write-ups  
• 更新 (“renewal/update”) – Japanese headline marker for “new/upgraded” developments, especially in political or municipal news  
• eva (subword piece) – the token-part that often signals proper names or dateline locations (“Geneva”) in wire stories  
• progression – a biomedical scoring or metric term (“cell cycle progression score”) in clinical research titles
This neuron fires whenever the model reads a single CJK “Han” character (Japanese‐style kanji or Chinese ideograph), flagging tokens from that logographic script.

This neuron fires on tokens that signal the start of a new section or title—i.e. headings, article titles or structural labels (like “Looking,” “Female,” “Romans,” “Background ==========,” “Category Archives,” “Travel Updates,” “Genetic,” “Introduction,” etc.) across various document genres. It’s essentially a marker-of-heading detector.

This neuron lights up on metadiscourse and framing words—short, high-level “signposts” like matter, case, held, contrast, subject, talk, stuck, it, here—that writers use to structure, frame, or shift topics in formal/expository prose.

This neuron is essentially a “scientific‐title detector.”  It lights up on the big, domain-specific noun/adjective that kicks off a research‐paper heading (Genetic, Molecular, Hydrogen, etc.) and on the matching closing period, marking the bounds of a paper’s title or section heading across biology, chemistry, physics and engineering.
This feature picks out the adverb “far” when it appears in the idiomatic phrase “so far,” signaling a discourse-level status update or partial summary of progress.

This neuron is essentially a “start-of-section” detector: it lights up on line-initial, capitalized BPE subtokens (e.g. “Human,” “Sw,” “Squ,” “Dis”) that typically open a new paragraph, heading, or section across many domains.

This neuron is a kind of “label-token” detector: it lights up on the principal identifier that follows a numeric or ordinal qualifier.  In a legal heading it peaks on the key noun (“Judicial” after “Fourth”), and in math problems it fires on the single-letter variable (q, r, m, etc.) that follows or is governed by the numeric expression.

This neuron is acting as a “title/headline boundary” detector.  It lights up on the initial subword of a multi-word title or proper name (always a capitalized prefix like Ep- in Epigenetic, Ke- in Keith, Sch- in Schneier, Gre- in Greco, Phil- in Philadunkia, Kat- in Katana, the word site in “dating site” or “fan site,” etc.) and also on the final punctuation (the closing period) that marks the end of those headlines, paper titles or names.

explanations.explanation: This neuron fires on “label” tokens that name structural or metadata elements across code and config files—i.e. identifiers used as data‐container or interface/serialization annotations (dictionary tags in XML, the “dump” marker in decompiled headers, IBOutlet’s “Out,” JSON keys like “requested,” plist Importer/Browser entries, etc.).

This feature fires on the abbreviation tokens that introduce legal‐reporter citations (e.g. the “F.” in “F.2d,” “F.3d,” “F Supp.”, etc.), effectively flagging volume/series markers in court‐case citations.

This feature detects structured headings and titles—uppercase section labels, case captions, citation lines and other formatted header tokens that mark the start of new sections or documents across legal, academic, and reference texts.

This neuron is essentially a “question-prompt” detector.  It lights up on tokens that introduce or cue a problem/request—chiefly the interrogative “What” (and its variants), ordinal-placeholders in “n’th-term” questions, sequence cues like “comes next,” directive verbs (“Calculate,” “Evaluate,” “Divide,” etc.), and even code/config identifiers when they appear as part of a prompt—i.e. anything that marks the start of an instruction or question.

This neuron is essentially a detector for “subword-start” BPE pieces – it fires on the very first one- or two-character token of a word (in any language or domain), e.g. “üh” in German führen/Stühler, “Sl” in FlexSlider, “UN” in VOLUNTEERED, “sw” in swimwear, “F” in Fusion, “m” in sigmoid, etc.

This neuron fires on high-salience, topic-introducing or emphasis tokens—things like proper names (“Australia,” “Berkeley,” “Reuters”), headline or domain markers (“NL Central,” “developer”), emphatic adverbs (“highly,” “randomized”) and even casual salutations (“Hey”). In other words, it flags words that kick off a new section, headline or topic.

This neuron is basically a “dot” detector – it fires on the period token (.) wherever it shows up as a boundary or namespace separator: end-of-sentence stops, domain/URL delimiters, package-name dots in code, XML tag breaks, file-extension markers, disambiguation entry endings, etc.

This neuron fires on the kind of Latin‐derived, abstract technical terms you see in scientific and technical writing—especially nominalizations and derivative adjectives ending in suffixes like ­ion, ­ity, ­ive, ­ance, etc. (e.g. “association,” “allocation,” “differential,” “conduction,” “equivalence,” “absolute,” “discontinuity”).

explanations.explanation: This feature fires on subword fragments that signal affixation or compounding—especially common prefixes (in-, re-, up-, well-, etc.) and hyphenated joins—i.e. the bits of tokens that mark morphological prefixes or hyphen boundaries.

This feature fires on “headline” or topic‐setting nouns—typically mass or plural forms—that name the central entities in a passage (e.g. professions or roles like landlords, architects, doctors, nurses, researchers, policymakers/providers; demographic groups like mothers, women; and domain subjects like asbestos, dolphins, CNTs, hospitals). It marks the key actor, group or subject around which the text is organized.

explanations.explanation: This neuron fires on “section-marker” tokens that introduce or label new blocks in technical text or code—framework or language names (Rails), override calls (super), error-type prefixes (ImportError:, TypeError:), URL schemes (://), transitional or dispatch words (Anyways/ways), status words (working), date headings (2018), etc.—all of which typically sit at the start of questions, answers, code snippets or blog-post sections.

This neuron lights up on those little in-word orthographic marks – soft-hyphens and accented vowels – that signal subword splits or diacritics (e.g. “Sep­tember,” “son-in-law,” “carboxy­methyl,” “evalúan,” “dúvida”). It’s essentially detecting non-ASCII hyphens and accent marks inside words across multiple languages.

This feature picks out Wikipedia’s structural “footer” markers—section headings like “External links” and the “Category: …” syntax (including the “in” in category names). It fires whenever the model encounters those article metadata/navigation tokens.

This feature is a detector for common Greek/Latin‐derived suffixes (and similar affixes) that form technical or scientific terms—e.g. –ography (imaging), –ase (enzymes), –psin (proteins), –osis (diseases), –class, –incision, –kDa, “.lite”/“.db” file extensions, “–less,” etc.—across biomedical, engineering, code and related domains. It lights up on those characteristic endings that signal specialized vocabulary.

This neuron fires on the “.” full‐stop token when it’s being used to terminate a sentence or clause (including in common abbreviations like “U.S.” or “e.g.”), effectively marking end-of-sentence punctuation.

explanations.explanation: This feature flags generic category nouns for tangible “products” or “goods” in listing/review contexts (e.g. model, shoes, baked goods, wigs, planes, cosmetics, etc.).
This feature detects the stock “…invention relates to…” phrase in patent‐style texts, i.e. the connective that introduces the invention’s subject or scope in patent abstracts.
This neuron is a “name‐piece” detector: it lights up on subword tokens that belong to proper nouns (people’s names, place names, org names, etc.) in news/Wikipedia‐style text.

This neuron fires on the very “front‐matter” of a document or code file – the formal header or title block (e.g. case captions and docket info in court opinions, license and copyright comments in source, config‐block names like MathJax, file‐name/metadata lines, etc.).

This feature detects recurring subword morphemes—especially IUPAC/biochemical affixes and other Greek-Latin roots (e.g. –oprop–, –glut–, –acetyl–, –mit–, –henyl–, –uring–, etc.)—that occur in the middle of long technical terms (chemical names, medical jargon, specialized code paths), effectively marking internal morpheme boundaries in domain-specific vocabulary.

This neuron fires on “boundary” tokens—punctuation marks (especially periods/full stops in sentences, numbers, domain or package names, and full-width variants in CJK text) and short subword clusters that typically kick off or appear in technical/brand terms (e.g. the “qu” in JQUERY or ACQUISITION, “cra” in craze, “dq” in a domain). In other words, it marks orthographic or lexical boundaries in mixed natural-and-code contexts.

This neuron lights up on those formulaic “status/action” words in formal technical or legal writing—i.e. adverbs (–ly), past-participle/adjectival forms (–ed, “illustrated,” “renewed,” “molded,” “reviewed,” “calculated,” “estimated,” “changed,” “used,” “known,” etc.) and key nouns like “copy.” In other words, it detects derivational morphology and passive/descriptor tokens typical of the impersonal, procedural style of scientific, patent or license documents.

explanations.explanation: This neuron fires whenever the model sees a word-piece that is “inside” a larger word (i.e. a continuation/subword fragment in BPE/WordPiece tokenization), regardless of language or script.

This feature fires on “know” when it marks an explicit admission or request of missing information—i.e. an epistemic‐uncertainty cue (“I don’t know…,” “we don’t know…,” “if you don’t know…,” etc.) across diverse topics.
This feature is a sentence‐boundary detector. It lights up on end-of-sentence punctuation (full stops) and on the first token of the next sentence (e.g. a capitalized word like “Everyone”).

This neuron fires whenever the model hits the head of a noun‐phrase that’s introducing an abstract concept or procedural/topic chunk (e.g. “process,” “path,” “story,” “depravity,” “decipher,” or the enumerator “or”), i.e. the key noun (or connective) that launches an explanatory or thematic segment.
